Feast On This Art World Roast
Hyperallergic skewers the art world and serves it up for your Thanksgiving feast. Also, artist Kohar Avakian eulogizes the ancestor whose legacy lives on.

This year, as the American holiday takes on new levels of monstrosity amid USA 250 propaganda, we’re marking it in the best way we know how: with a healthy serving of gratitude and satire. Let’s start with the second one — because what’s Thanksgiving without a pageant? Enjoy our full art-world roast, starring MoMA as the sad, white turkey meat and the Breuer Building as the dreaded turducken. Dig in!

Meanwhile, artist and scholar Kohar Avakian approaches the day by turning her attention toward a figure whose life was largely left out of the historical record: Cuff Annum. The enslaved Black man, who would serve in the Revolutionary War, became a common ancestor for a lineage of African-American and Native families in Massachusetts. Avakian, one of his descendants, lingers on the archive’s failure to capture his legacy and answers that gap with her own visual art.

And in the spirit of gratitude, we asked artists, art workers, and other community members we know to reflect on what they’re thankful for as 2026 draws to a close. Writer Christina Sharpe sums it up best: “All of the ways of being for each other when fascism wants to individuate, hierarchize, and isolate fill me with gratitude.” And we’re thankful for you, dear reader, wherever you are today.

Yes, it’s a day to be surrounded by those you love, even if some topics may be taboo at the dinner table. But what’s love without conflict? Hyperallergic is not one to appease those who deserve a light ribbing, particularly in an art world that prides itself on being so cutting-edge and consequential — for better or worse.

So, we’ve chosen to whet your appetites a little before your big meal by roasting our dear art community and reminding us all that laughter and humor are integral to how we digest the world and its many foibles and maddening realities.

‘Pay attention and stay curious’: Réka Matyas on her charming little worlds filled with spotty dogs and…
The Budapest-based illustrator fills her colourful drawings with curious characters and unexpected details, encouraging us to slow down and find joy in the everyday. Spend a few minutes in…
The Budapest-based illustrator fills her colourful drawings with curious characters and unexpected details, encouraging us to slow down and find joy in the everyday.

Spend a few minutes in Réka Mátyás ’ portfolio, and you’ll meet two spotty dogs gazing at each other across a green meadow, a polka-dot cat posing beside an equally polka-dot tabi shoe, and a woman with ladybugs crawling through her golden hair. Polka-dot sisters, three cats stretched out across a chocolate-brown page, and a figure cradling a birthday cake with a single lit candle appear. It all feels soft, warm and slightly odd, splashed in a playful palette of bubblegum pinks, grassy greens and buttery yellows.

The Budapest-based illustrator and motion designer was born in Transylvania, Romania, and began her creative journey at university, where she studied Fine Arts and graduated with a BA in 2022. She experimented with all sorts of materials and mediums, though pencil sketches and realistic drawing were her real loves. By the end of her degree, she admits, she “felt quite lost”, with plenty of pressure to find her own style. So she took a year off and landed a role at a small creative studio as a motion designer, where she picked up the software, dabbled in graphic design, and started to see new possibilities. That led her to Budapest for a master’s in Graphic Design, which she completed in 2025. Today, she works full-time as a motion designer at Artbinary, “an amazing agency where I feel like part of the family”, while illustration fills her free time, along with the occasional graphic design project when something resonates.

For a long while, Réka felt she had to pick one path out of the three. “It stressed me out quite a bit,” she says. “But over time, I’ve learned to embrace all three, and I finally feel like I’ve found my place. I’ve also realised that switching between them keeps me creatively fresh. Each discipline gives me a different perspective and a little breathing room from the others, allowing me to return to my work with new ideas and push it in directions I might not have discovered otherwise. Now, rather than seeing these different paths as competing with each other, I see them as things that feed into and strengthen one another.”

With the world around her as her muse, Réka’s ideas usually come from everyday moments. “I’m interested in observing people, their lives and the little moments that might seem insignificant at first,” she says. Réka then jots these observations down or makes quick sketches in a notebook, where an idea might sit for months before it finds its way into an illustration. Nature, music, films and whatever book she’s reading chip in too, because “you just have to pay attention and stay curious”.

When the time comes to make something, Réka sits quietly for a few minutes and lets her mind wander, imagining a little scenario around the theme. Then comes lots of tiny, rough pencil or coloured-pen sketches. “They’re usually pretty ugly, and I almost always hate all of them at first!” she laughs, but this messy stage is where the final concept tends to appear, often somewhere completely different from where she started. Once something feels right, she plays with the composition, mood and colour, then moves to her iPad, which she says is usually the quickest part.

Among her favourites is an illustration for ZEITmagazine, commissioned by art director Viola Hasse, and her first editorial job. She had never drawn older people before, so she dived straight into sketching, starting with the couple at the centre – looking lovingly into each other’s eyes – and building a story around them with symbols and perspectives. Look closely, and you’ll spot a bird with a broken wing, which denotes the woman’s gradual loss of independence; pills; a pair of glasses; a water droplet and a character looking longingly in the distance. “I wanted the storytelling to feel subtle, rather than too literal, with little details that you could discover as you looked at the image,” she says. “I really enjoyed finding ways to translate the different layers of the story into small visual elements.”
Pattern Coffee is what happens when a Belfast branding studio becomes its own client
Fluent Format’s David Lewis on Pattern Coffee, the Belfast speciality coffee brand he’s built with Andile Cebekhulu as a side project, and what it taught them about clients. I’m a big fan…
Fluent Format’s David Lewis on Pattern Coffee, the Belfast speciality coffee brand he’s built with Andile Cebekhulu as a side project, and what it taught them about clients.

I’m a big fan of side projects. Creative Boom began as one, and look at it now. It seems I’m not alone. Every studio has one. The passionate thing on the side that gets talked about on a Friday afternoon, sketched out on paper, and then quietly forgotten about when Monday’s deadlines come in.

David Lewis and Andile Cebekhulu actually made theirs come true. David is the founder and creative director of Belfast brand and digital consultancy Fluent Format; Andile is its lead developer. By day, the pair build brands and digital experiences for other people. Alongside all that, they’ve been finding the time to build Pattern Coffee, a speciality coffee brand of their own.

Much like my platform, it began with no plan to be a business at all. The two friends spent nine months sourcing and trying coffees from around the world before deciding there was an opportunity. “We’re both dads with young families, busy jobs and a real love of coffee,” says David. “We joke that coffee is what keeps us going, but it’s also something we genuinely enjoy.”

What’s with the name, though? It came about during a phone call after work, when the pair got talking about how coffee had become part of their daily ritual – a moment to step away, reset and go again. Cue Pattern, along with a brand philosophy, ‘Your daily sweet spot’.
Graphic designers spend their working lives telling clients that brand matters. So can you imagine the pressure when it’s your own name on the packaging, and your own money behind it?

“We’ve always believed that a great brand can make a real difference to a business,” says David. “It’s not just about having a nice logo or packaging. It’s about creating something people recognise, connect with and want to be part of. Pattern gave us the chance to connect with and want to be part of. It gave us the chance to explore that from the very beginning, with complete creative freedom.”

I’m familiar with that freedom. It lets you go crazy without constraints. For David and Andile, it showed up most in the packaging. Because rather than go for the usual coffee tin, they developed a sleeve that follows the same silhouette of the bag, so the overall shape stays the same while each batch of coffee gets its own visual identity.
“We knew how the bag looked on a shop shelf was just as important as how it looked on someone’s kitchen counter,” explains David. “We wanted to create something people would enjoy having around.”
Wings, rugby and a snowball effect

Amazingly, there’s been no traditional marketing. Instead, Pattern has grown through small brand activations, like collaborations with running clubs and gyms, and even pop-ups at chicken wing shops – not, I admit, where I expected a speciality coffee brand to show up. But there you go.
The pair has also sponsored grassroots rugby, including women’s sports events, schools and universities, and supported Cancer Fund for Children on several occasions.

“We’ve found that the smallest things often have the biggest impact,” says David. “One collaboration leads to another, someone discovers the coffee and shares it with a friend, and before you know it, there’s a real snowball effect. It’s allowed us to build the brand and community we always wanted, without forcing it.”

But speciality coffee can feel intimidating when you think of all the tasting notes and brew ratios. Pattern is having none of that. “We love good coffee, but we don’t think you should have to know everything about it to enjoy it,” David continues. “We wanted Pattern to feel approachable, welcoming and something everyone could be part of.”

So what are the lessons from running a coffee brand on the side when you build brands for a living? Quite a lot. “It’s been a proper hustle getting it off the ground,” says David. “When you’re the one sourcing products, packing orders and investing your own money, you develop a completely different appreciation for the start-up founders you work with.”

Why Victorious Festival stopped selling its headliners and started selling Portsmouth
Portsmouth’s August bank holiday festival had a bit of a problem. Too many people were buying a ticket for one act on one day, then disappearing. Wildish & Co.’s solution is an identity…

Portsmouth’s August bank holiday festival had a bit of a problem. Too many people were buying a ticket for one act on one day, then disappearing. Wildish & Co.’s solution is an identity that puts the city first.

Who doesn’t love a good festival? I’ve been to my fair share over the last thirty years, and I can always tell you which bands were playing. The Prodigy in 1995 and Bowie in 2000, both at Glastonbury. Cypress Hill at V Festival in 2022 along with Asian Dub Foundation, I think it was. Björk at Bluedot a few years ago. Fun times.

If you’re running an event like this, you’ll know a lot hangs on your line-up. If it isn’t good enough, people simply won’t book. Victorious Festival knows this only too well. For more than a decade, the three-day event on Southsea seafront has drawn crowds from across the south of England, including Kings of Leon, Jamiroquai and Kasabian. But many of those only bought a ticket for a particular day, saw their fave act and went home. As such, each day felt like a different crowd, and that transience can be hard to build a community around.

Cue London agency Wildish & Co., which has given Victorious a new brand strategy, verbal identity and visual system that helps sell the festival as more than its line-up. Yeah, the headliners are still there - Black Eyed Peas, Pet Shop Boys and The Kooks are on the 2027 bill – but they’re no longer the sole attraction. Portsmouth is.

The idea is to sell the weekend , not just one day or act. Which is why the new positioning makes sense: ‘The People’s Classic’. It’s a line inspired by the ones who keep coming back, from families and festival veterans to traders, volunteers and first-timers. A second line, ‘Portsmouth Says Welcome’, ties the brand to the city that hosts it. Perfect.

It’s smart because you can’t own a line-up but you can own a seafront, a city, and something to look forward to every August. It’s something no rival festival can compete with. If you shift the story from who’s on stage to where you actually are and who you’re with, then a day ticket starts to look like you’re missing out.

The history behind the festival is also lovely. Victorious grew out of Portsmouth’s own music scene – its founders previously ran local venue Little Johnny Russell’s – and the new strategy includes a celebration of those humble roots.

Going back to the warm welcome, who’s it for? The identity launches alongside the 2027 line-up with large-scale posters at London Waterloo, Clapham Junction and Brighton, which shows you the target market.

Looking at the logo, it swaps the O in Victorious for a starburst borrowed from the sun on Portsmouth’s own coat of arms. Will you look at that – the city is quite literally in the middle of the name. The starburst also acts as an icon and is used across social, merchandise, wristbands and wayfinding.

There’s a custom headline typeface called Victorious Bold, which has tall, narrow capitals which stand out beautifully on everything from posters to stage screens. And the palette is taken right off the seafront – Navy, Sky, Sunset and Sunrise colours are complemented by secondary hues such as Sun Burn, Sea Spray and Sea Weed. A wave device runs through the lot, framing tickets, flags and signage. This was clearly a fun brief.

Then there are the illustrations, drawn in an engraving style and celebrating people enjoying themselves: a crab in headphones, for example, plus a sandcastle built from speakers and a seagull in a bucket hat. Remember those? Bucket hats were very handy when you needed to roll something out of the wind. Ahem.

A really nice touch is that every artist’s press photo gets a custom risograph-inspired treatment, so every act looks like part of the same thing. In other words, the headliners have been made to fit into Victorious’s world, when it has previously been the other way round.

Is the client happy? “Wildish & Co. got Victorious straight away,” says Leah Hennessy-Williams, head of PR and marketing at the festival. “They understood that what makes this festival special isn’t just who’s on stage, it’s the sea air, the city and the people who come back every single year. Freytag Anderson serves up branding with bounce for a Scottish padel startup
The Glasgow studio built the Edinburgh company’s brand from the ground up, from naming to rackets. If you haven’t heard of padel yet, don’t worry: your life will be fine without it. At the…
The Glasgow studio built the Edinburgh company’s brand from the ground up, from naming to rackets.

If you haven’t heard of padel yet, don’t worry: your life will be fine without it. At the same time, it’s nice to know that this trendy racket sport, which is kind of a cross between tennis and squash, is making a lot of people very happy right now; mainly in North America, but increasingly in the UK too.

Inevitably, there’s already a crowded market of kit brands all competing for padel fans’ attention. And the latest to catch our attention, at least, is CCO: an Edinburgh-based startup aiming to become a premium international padel brand.
This new brand has been crafted from the start by Glasgow studio Freytag Anderson, four-time winner of Scottish Design Agency of the Year.

Their work has included naming, positioning, visual identity, product architecture, racket design, and packaging, while for the website and e-commerce side, they teamed up with Form , a studio based in Aberdeen and Glasgow.

Readers of Creative Boom might read CCO as “Chief Creative Officer”, but that’s not what most padel players will think in practice. In any case, the name here is an acronym for “Control Creates Opportunity”. That will make perfect sense to fans of the game, where patience and placement tend to beat brute force.
The overall positioning of the brand, meanwhile, blends technical performance with a refined, lifestyle-led feel. This is captured simply but precisely in the tagline: “Performance. Synced.”

At the heart of the visual identity is a stepped typemark inspired by the movement of a padel ball. The two Cs and the O read almost like frames from a slow-motion replay, as if the ball is gradually coming into focus.

It’s a simple idea, but it’s been executed brilliantly, and is flexible enough to stretch across the brand’s three racket ranges, along with balls, apparel and accessories. The design particularly comes to life on the rackets themselves, where the mark is stacked, mirrored and multiplied to create bold, radiating patterns that echo the rhythm of the game.
A similar use of pattern repetition carries across to the campaign images, captured by Edinburgh-based photographer Murray Orr, in which players appear in staggered, multiple-exposure frames.

The colour palette – mostly blacks, whites and greys – evokes an understated, premium feel. This, along with the clean, sans-serif typography and restraint, helps the brand stand out in a sporting category not known for its subtlety.

“For the digital experience, we brought in Cameron Fraser and Kyle McKenzie at Form Digital ,” says Daniel Fretag, creative director at Freytag Anderson. “They’re exceptionally good at what they do, particularly when it comes to creating thoughtful, intuitive digital experiences that also work commercially. Together we translated the brand into a Shopify-powered e-commerce platform.”

Which museum is a white-meat turkey, which is a sad side salad, and who's riding the gravy train this holiday season?

Yes, it’s a day to be surrounded by those you love, even if some topics may be taboo at the dinner table. But what’s love without conflict? Hyperallergic is not one to appease those who deserve a light ribbing, particularly in an art world that prides itself on being so cutting-edge and consequential — for better or worse.

So, we’ve chosen to whet your appetites a little before your big meal by roasting our dear art community and reminding us all that laughter and humor are integral to how we digest the world and its many foibles and maddening realities.

The Museum of Modern Art’s refusal to let go of its billionaire trustee is the saddest, yet least surprising thing ever. A museum birthed and continually fed by the ultra-rich and their scions might be the poster child of neoliberal America, no matter how many women-focused, BIPOC, or queer programs they support in what essentially is a “let them eat cake” approach to equity. But cake is too sweet for this lot, even if its richness may be fitting, so we’ve decided to give them the plump spot of white turkey meat on today’s roast. Like the tryptophan-rich poultry, MoMA’s political hypocrisy makes us want to take a nap.

Nothing ruins Thanksgiving like a bland, butterless, suspiciously pale lump of mashed potatoes; perhaps the same is true of Alma Allen’s soulless sculptures at the just-closed Venice Biennale. The spineless presentation at the United States pavilion was the (tasteless) product of the State Department’s reported involvement in the art exhibition. All that’s left to say is: Pass the salt!

Though it's a beautiful deep berry color, there’s always too much cranberry sauce — and when it’s passed around the table, everyone politely says, "No, thank you." That’s why we deem Pace Gallery to be the cranberry sauce: There are too many locations, too many pretty colors, and no one wants any of it, especially the 50 staffers and 50 artists who were laid off and cut from the roster this June.

Basquiat’s Paintings Reveal Hidden Images Under UV Light in New Miami Exhibition
A post shared by Jean-Michel Basquiat: King Pleasure© (@basquiatkingpleasure)

In a focused exhibition for Art Week Miami , a previously unseen side of Jean-Michel Basquiat’s artwork is finally coming to light in Basquiat. A Hidden World . The show highlights Basquiat’s use of ultraviolet (UV) materials, bringing together four of his paintings that contain hidden images and markings invisible to the naked eye. The exhibition offers a new look at Basquiat’s creative process, revealing that there may be more to some of his most recognizable works than meets the eye.

Opening Nov. 29 at the Institute of Contemporary Art (ICA) Miami, the exhibition is the first dedicated specifically to Basquiat’s use of UV materials. With the help of specialized lighting, visitors will be able to see a completely different side of paintings that, under normal lighting, appear much simpler.

One of the most striking examples is Emblem , a painting from 1984. Under normal light, the painting features a largely white background with scattered figures and markings. However, when illuminated with UV light, the canvas is transformed, revealing a vibrant collection of hidden drawings, words, and symbols. Among them is the phrase “invisible men,” which the exhibition’s catalogue connects to the underrepresentation and erasure of Black people in art.

Interestingly enough, Basquiat was already known for his tendency to paint over or partially erase parts of his work, often leaving traces of what had been there before. “I scratch out and erase but never so much that they don’t know what was there. My version of pentimento,” the artist once said. Pentimento is a term used to describe earlier layers of a painting that become visible beneath the final image. With his use of UV materials, Basquiat took this practice a step further, creating entire layers that could only be seen under certain lighting conditions.

Other works featured in the exhibition include Untitled (Orange Sports Figure) from 1982, which contains Basquiat’s signature and date in invisible ink, as well as Cash crop and O.M.R.A.V.S. , both completed in 1984. Together, the four paintings offer a closer look at how the artist experimented with different materials and played with the idea of what should be seen and what should remain hidden.

The exhibition is also working with art conservator Suzanne Siano to study the paintings and better understand the materials Basquiat used. These findings will be documented in an accompanying catalogue, offering further insight into an aspect of his work that has remained hidden for decades.

Curated by Dieter Buchhart and Anna Karina Hofbauer, Basquiat. A Hidden World will be on view at ICA Miami’s Expansion Space in the Design District through Feb. 15, 2027. For an artist whose work has been studied and celebrated for decades, the exhibition raises an interesting question: How much of Basquiat’s art have we really been seeing all this time?

As every self-help book will tell you, it's important to practice gratitude, especially in the darkest times. Unraveling Thanksgiving's history as a tribute to Indigenous dispossession, this week is a time to do just that — give thanks for the support and solidarity that keeps us going. This year, we invited artists, writers, and art workers from our extended community to share what and whom they're thankful for. They shouted out their friends, students, favorite artworks, books, and more. Their contributions fill us with hope and faith in the future, and for that we're grateful.

Seeing Lorna Simpson’s “Wigs” in a study room with my students at the Museum of Modern Art is an experience in the auratic mysteries of the object: its ability to speak, mutely and persistently. Are we looking at an heirloom catalog or a series of specimens, evidence of female choice, or racial fetishization? The ethical dilemma underlying the very notion of collecting haunts museums themselves as institutional repositories of imperial and colonial appetite. Yet, given our current political moment when inconvenient histories are being systemically and institutionally erased, museums also provide spaces for critical remembrance, crucial holders of the past and how that past continues to shape our present. I remain grateful to those museums today who see education and critical analysis as integral parts of their mission.

PS — Is it a coincidence that institutions are starving the humanities and the arts just when common human decency and the ideal of a common good are radically disintegrating? Art matters precisely for its ability to articulate and invoke the ineffable. Think these lines from William Carlos Williams:

Tending the Legacy of Cuff Annum, Ancestor of Black and Native Worcester
Like thousands of other Black and Native American soldiers in the Revolutionary War, Cuff risked his life for the faulty promise of freedom and land for his family. Because of him, I am…

The American Revolution did not begin with a “shot heard ’round the world.” Three days before the Battles of Lexington and Concord, the rebellion started with a secret. On April 16, 1775, Isaiah Thomas and Timothy Bigelow smuggled a wooden printing press across the moonlit Charles River, from Boston to Worcester, Massachusetts, the ancestral homelands of the Nipmuc people. Their clandestine mission salvaged Thomas’s patriot newspaper, The Massachusetts Spy , which published the first eyewitness accounts of the revolution.

Soon, both men became celebrated founding fathers in New England. Bigelow sheltered the printing press and hosted Sons of Liberty meetings in his Worcester home. He commanded the 15th Massachusetts Regiment and soldiered alongside George Washington at Valley Forge. On July 14, 1776, Thomas reportedly delivered the region’s first public reading of the Declaration of Independence in Worcester. In 1812, Thomas compiled his personal collection and founded the American Antiquarian Society , the nation’s oldest and largest historical society today.

And yet, triumphant narratives like these — particularly amid the country’s 250th anniversary this year — elide the cruel hypocrisies of American independence. As Bigelow battled alongside Black and Native soldiers, he enslaved people in private. As Thomas championed freedom, he published advertisements for the recapture of “runaways.” But this story is not about Bigelow or Thomas. There are enough monuments and collections dedicated in their honor.

This is a belated elegy for Cuff Annum — father, husband, and soldier in Bigelow’s regiment. Cuff became a common ancestor of a long, braided lineage of Black and Native families from central Massachusetts. After Cuff’s death, Hagar, his widow, became head of the largest household of color on Back Street (now Summer) in Worcester. Their daughter Dinah married twice. From one of these marriages, I am a direct descendant. Because Cuff Annum lived, I am alive today.

Photographer Shares the Emotional Story Behind an Elephant Carrying Its Stillborn Calf [Interview]

Wildlife photographer Federico Veronesi encountered the shot of a lifetime in Damaraland, Namibia. In September 2025, he witnessed a desert elephant carrying its stillborn calf. What resulted was an arresting black-and-white image that is beautifully composed but ultimately full of grief. The close-up portrait shows the mother with her deceased calf between her tusk and trunk, as if she is unable to let her baby go. The emotional image, titled The Aftermath , was recognized in the prestigious Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 competition , with Veronesi earning the title of Overall Winner and the Behavior Mammals category winner.

Veronesi was tracking elephants when he noticed an unusual pattern of drag marks in the sand of a dry riverbed. He understood why when he saw the mother and child. “The calf’s body rose up and in this particular frame, it almost looks like the calf is still alive, playing with its mother or trying to cling to her mother’s trunk,” he recalls to My Modern Met. “I feel that the ambiguity of the image, and how it can be read in many ways make it stand out from the other images I took, where the calf is clearly hanging lifeless from the mother’s tusk.”

The photographer initially felt conflicted about capturing the scene. “After taking the first few images, I felt like I was violating the elephant’s intimate moment, her grief, I was almost ashamed and thought that I shouldn’t take these photographs,” he shares. But ultimately, Veronesi found it important to highlight the complexity of these creatures. Elephants have been observed engaging in behaviors around death, including vocalizing, guarding the deceased, and carrying the dead, as pictured. By photographing this painful moment, Veronesi shows us that wildlife and humans aren’t as far apart as we may think.
We spoke with Veronesi about capturing the poignant shot, his philosophy about photographing wildlife, and more. Scroll down for My Modern Met’s exclusive interview.
What is your photography background, and how did you begin photographing wildlife?

Photography was part of my life since an early age as I grew up in a family of keen nature photographers. Every travel or outing was always centered on photographing nature, birds and wildlife in particular. I therefore learned photography almost naturally. I began photographing wildlife with my Polaroid on my first trip to Africa when I was 6 years old or to the local zoos and safari parks. During my teenage years I upgraded to a reflex camera and slides, and that’s what I used for my first years in Kenya after I moved there in 2002 to follow my dream of living among wildlife and photographing it full time.
Set up the scene for your image The Aftermath , which shows an elephant carrying a dead calf. How did you come across this?

I was in Damaraland, northwestern Namibia, with the specific aim to photograph desert-adapted elephants and other wildlife living in this particularly dry but stunning ecosystem. Elephants are frequently found along the dry riverbeds that traverse this landscape, as that’s where they find some trees and vegetation that they can feed on. I had seen a family of elephants the previous evening, so that morning I returned to the place where I left them to pick up their tracks and hopefully find them again. As I followed the tracks, I noticed an unusual dragging mark on the ground, which I wasn’t immediately able to interpret. Shortly after I finally came across the elephants feeding on the river banks. Out of the group, a female appeared carrying a dead calf by wedging the calf’s leg between her trunk and tusk.
How did the final image emerge? Did you realize the photograph’s importance when you snapped it?

As the scene appeared in front of me, I grabbed my 400mm telephoto lens and framed the images, I went for a vertical crop as she was coming towards me and she filled the frame nicely. As she came forward, another elephant was following her, so she abruptly turned away. Run with the Semi-Wild Yilki Horses of Anatolia in Nur Tucker’s Captivating Photos
In 'The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse,' the British-Turkish photographer captures a portrait of the region's living heritage.

Around the dusty plains and otherworldly volcanic rock formations of the historical region of Cappadocia , a millennia-old tradition continues. Here in Central Anatolia, Turkey, horses have been a part of daily life, civic programs, and military campaigns since prehistory. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse , photographer Nur Tucker captures a portrait of the region’s living heritage.

Published by Hemeria, the title delves into the beauty and tenacity of the semi-wild horses while also highlighting the lifestyles of those who herd them through rugged landscapes. Tucker, who is a British-Turkish photographer based in the U.K., has long been drawn to the vigor and elegance of horses, and the yilki breed that populates Anatolia have a particularly resonant history.

“Yilki” comes from the Turkish verb yılmak , which means “to flee” or “to be set loose.” The name “has come to describe the condition of these herds that live between liberation and loss, between domestic heritage and wild abandon,” says a statement.

In a place where horses have been bred for agriculture, transportation, battle, and more for thousands of years, their role forever changed within just the past century due to mechanization and industrialization. With motorized tractors, trucks, and cars to work the fields and provide transportation, horses essentially became redundant. Released to fend for themselves, they survived harsh winters, bred on their own, and grew into sizable herds. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, Tucker composes a love letter to these striking animals, celebrating their resilience through more than 100 images.
The book is available for purchase directly from Hemeria , and it’s slated for worldwide release next October. See more on Tucker’s Instagram .

Andrew Hopgood is an Australian artist from Melbourne whose practice brings together illustration, oil painting and sculpture.
Andrew Hopgood is a member of the Beautiful Bizarre Artist Directory

Andrew Hopgood is an Australian artist from Melbourne whose practice brings together illustration, oil painting and sculpture. Having started his artistic journey in illustration, he expanded into painting and sculpture around 2019, developing a visual language that combines realism with subtle surrealist elements. Much of his work centres on the natural world, particularly endangered species and the challenges wildlife faces as its environment continues to change. Through carefully constructed compositions, Andrew captures the beauty and presence of animals while drawing attention to their vulnerability and the importance of protecting the world they inhabit.

A defining feature of Andrew’s work is the way he blurs the boundaries between reality and fantasy. His compositions often place familiar elements of nature within imagined settings, creating scenes that feel at once recognizable and otherworldly.

These dreamlike environments allow him to explore the environmental pressures affecting wildlife while also considering the possibility of adaptation and survival. Rather than focusing solely on the loss and uncertainty surrounding endangered species, He introduces subtle moments of hope, imagining a natural world that continues to find ways forward. Through this balance of realism and imagination, he encourages viewers to look more closely at the relationship between humans and the environment, and to consider the role we play in shaping its future.

Joa Vilallonga is a Peruvian American contemporary artist based in Florida. She completed coursework at the Escuela Nacional de Bellas Artes in Lima before earning a BFA in Illustration, summa cum laude, from the Fashion Institute of Technology in New York. In 2017, she received FIT’s Antonio López Alumni Grant.

Her practice spans painting, sculpture, and poetry, with figurative portraiture at its core. Through layered surfaces and restrained tonal transitions, she creates a contemplative atmosphere that defines her visual language. Her paintings unfold as an exploration of stillness, perception, and emotional presence. Her work has been presented in group exhibitions in New York, Tokyo, and Tbilisi. She is a member of Unearthed, an invitation-only community for artists working in analogue, handmade media.

Joa Vilallonga’s paintings explore liminal states beyond linear time, opening visual fields where stillness becomes active. Working within contemporary figuration, she approaches portraiture as a psychological landscape. Her figures merge subtly with their surroundings, inhabiting states of silent depth. Rooted in a self-contained feminine presence, they neither seek approval nor resolution; vulnerability and strength coexist without performance.

Natural elements such as water, wind, gravity, and light function as compositional forces. Water plays a central role in her imagery, suggesting fluidity and receptivity. The human form appears permeable, shaped by transitions that soften boundaries and slow perception. Animals and small organic forms act as quiet counterparts, grounding what cannot be directly spoken.
Through restrained composition, muted palettes, and subtle luminosity, she builds contemplative images that invite sustained attention while leaving interpretation open.

A Sculptural Playground in Shanghai Is Designed for Human-Powered Play
Jump onto Wade and Leta's sculptural design in Shanghai.

In Shanghai’s Jing’an Sculpture Park, a monumental new installation by Brooklyn’s Wade and Leta has a clear goal: to get people up and moving in the same space. Titled “Catching Feelings,” the interactive artwork doubles as an all-ages playground with the artists’ signature sculptures and geometric forms. A central tower holds a quartet of slides, while other spinning and writhing elements are designed for more unstructured interaction.

“Catching Feelings” is one of 36 projects in the ninth edition of the Jing’an International Sculpture Project, an annual project helmed by the UCCA Center for Contemporary Art . In comparison to the artists’ earlier works , the bold, kinetic playground is decidedly analog, with any movement powered by the people interacting with its components rather than embedded motors or motion generated by the wind.

“We’re interested in the life and activity around our work—the behaviors it causes, the elations it brings,” the artists say in a statement. “We watched the same grandfather return with his granddaughter to play hide and seek; an 84-year-old and his partner used the space as the backdrop for their video recordings; new friends were made on our ground spinners; we even glimpsed a man in a business suit having a go on the slide.”

“Catching Feelings” is presented alongside monumental works by Olafur Eliasson , Marshmallow Laser Feast , and many others on view through December 31. Find more from Wade and Leta on their Instagram .

The New York-based artist combines delicate pencil drawings with the nostalgic graphics of the early internet, exploring intimacy and the blurry line between what’s real and what’s artificial.

A swallow perches on a white plastic garden chair beside a column of blue folder icons, apparently waiting for a download to finish. A pale sky lifted from a computer desktop frames a bird circled in red under the instruction “Enter the following”, and the answer typed in the box below reads “birds :-)”. In her artworks, Gigi Borgese draws every detail by hand, and the gentle humour really rises to the surface once you know where it all comes from.

Growing up in San Jose, California, Gigi describes herself as largely self-taught, having spent much of her life as what she calls “a passive creative”. Between the ages of 14 and 17, she was an influencer on early TikTok, where the objectification she endured and “the feelings of emptiness/futility in that content” pushed her to delete her accounts and commit to art.

She spent a year at West Valley Community College, then moved to New York in 2023 at 19. She now studies for a BFA in Studio Art at the City College of New York, with a minor in Classics, and has won the Adelaide Jablonsky Award (2025) and the Connor Merritt Award (2026). She was also a finalist in the 2026 Astor Place student art competition, and alongside her degree, she works at the Morris Jumel Mansion on public programming, prop recreation and research.

Her subject matter took shape in 2025, when she was 20. Unknown numbers began texting her doctored and AI-generated images of herself, often depicting her as a minor. “I quickly discovered an active Discord group of over 100 men who had been doing this to me for, at the time, five years,” she says. It sent her back to her years as an influencer and to larger questions around human connection online. “I would not wish that on anyone; however, I credit this event for forcing me to figure out what I wanted to say with my art.”

What she wanted to say arrives through birds, apples and flowers, forms she associates with fragility and femininity, which she then “bastardises” with the visual language of the internet. At 18, she saw Sonya Rapoport’s exhibition Force fields at the Minnesota Street Project in San Francisco, and the artist’s continuous-feed computer paper and early ASCII art “resonated with a part of me that had not yet processed the impact that the internet had on me.”

She’s also drawn to Plato’s ideas about reality and representation. “If the physical world is a flawed copy of our internal world, then the internet is a further copied and flawed version of the physical world.” That chain of copies becomes literal in her work, where you see a swallow multiplying into fading outlines, as if copied and pasted; and a pixelated bird hovering over two ordinary swallows on a yellow grid; and a row of halved green apples placed with the caption “Forbidden (What does it feel like?)”.

To build these scenes, she browses dead websites and old web interfaces, then looks at 19th-century scientific illustrations of flowers and birds. “I find similarity in this artificial attempt to capture the essence of something true,” she says. She works like one of those illustrators, “crudely recreating something with influences from digital spaces”, a method that deliberately mirrors the way the men copied her.

Beautiful Bastard (2026), the piece she says she's proudest of, started when she felt stuck in her older work. Using coloured pencil, graphite, and Micron pen on pastel paper, she draws a poppy “plainly” on the left, and beside it looms a “monstrous, saturated, pixelated imitation of its form”, slightly larger and distorted, yet trapped inside a strict grid. “As the replications continue, the form loses its distinction and our experience with the object changes, becoming less sincere,” she explains.

A Kiss for the Love of my Life (2026) is a simpler piece made of coloured pencil, graphite and Micron pen on Strathmore drawing pad paper – it’s also a little quieter and more disturbing, featuring a swallow kissing a blank, expressionless figure who remains perfectly still. The drawing asks what…
Why Camille Walala is transforming a metro station with 30,000 hand-made tiles inspired by basketball
Alley-Oop, the French-born artist’s first permanent public artwork, pays tribute to a basketball legend and an architectural landmark. If you’ve spent any time in East London, you’ll…
Alley-Oop, the French-born artist’s first permanent public artwork, pays tribute to a basketball legend and an architectural landmark.

If you’ve spent any time in East London, you’ll probably have come across Camille Walala’s work, albeit perhaps unknowingly; from the Dream Come True Building on Old Street to the stretch of Leyton High Street she covered in grids, triangles and stripes.

Now the French-born, London-based artist is bringing her colourful, Memphis-influenced style to the platforms of Flachet–Alain Gilles metro station in Villeurbanne, part of greater Lyon, France, which serves around 5.7 million passengers a year.

Set for completion next Spring, the installation, titled Alley-Oop, has been created from more than 30,000 hand-crafted ceramic tiles. This will be the biggest project of Camille’s career to date. It’s also her first permanent public-realm work, her first major project in her home country and her first large-scale use of ceramic tile as a material.

Like the Memphis Group that inspires so much of her work – an Italian design and architecture group active from 1980 to 1987 – Camille believes the boundaries between art and everyday life should be porous, or even absent altogether, and that our surroundings should actively shape how we feel.

There are also two specific influences on Alley-Oop. Firstly, the title itself comes from the basketball move where one player throws the ball towards the hoop and a teammate catches it in mid-air and scores. And if you’re wondering what that has to do with rail transport, it’s a nod to the station’s namesake, Alain Gilles, who is considered one of the greatest players in the history of French basketball.

The energy of the basketball court can be clearly seen in the tiles themselves, with rebounding forms, repeated shapes and a rhythm that carries along the platform walls and columns. In a quite magical way, stacked, striped blocks and wavy lines seem to bounce off each other as you move through the space.

A second influence on Camille’s work here is architectural. The commune Villeurbanne is home to a striking 1980s building by Swiss postmodern architect Mario Botta, the MLIS (Maison du Livre, de l’Image et du Son), which features stark geometry, horizontal banding and a dramatic central lightwell.
These forms are echoed in Alley-Oop’s 3D-effect tile patterns, while the palette is said to match the vibrancy and confidence of the decade in which Botta’s building appeared.

“This project means a huge amount to me, and not only because it’s in France,” says Camille. “I have spent many years thinking about the role our environments play in shaping our emotions and behaviours, and my work is animated by the belief that art can drive genuine and meaningful change to our social wellbeing.

“People rarely think about how and what an environment like a metro station communicates with us, and they tend to be quite blank, colourless spaces as a result. With Alley-Oop, we have a wonderful opportunity to engage with the public visually and emotionally, turning a transient transport space into a place of discovery, contemplation and interaction.”
Camille has certainly put the hours in, having spent over four years working on the project to date, making it the most complex and ambitious project in the history of her studio.

She won the commission back in 2022 through an international competition run by Sytral Mobilités, the public transport authority for Lyon. Around 300 artists were in the running to upgrade this and three other stations: Foch, République Villeurbanne and Gratte-Ciel.

Since then, she’s been working alongside architects Atelier Martel, Paris-based art production studio Poïèma and engineering consultancy Betrec. The renovation work has been carried out at night, so that the station can remain open during the entire project. They’ll have spent more than nine months on site by the time it’s finished.

Until now, much of Camille’s best-known work has been temporary; Alley-Oop opens a new chapter for the artist. Fired into ceramic tiles and built into the fabric of the station, it’ll be part of daily life for commuters for…
Carling’s new identity is a badge of belonging inspired by its football ties
BrandOpus has refreshed the much-loved lager brand with a football-style crest celebrating its Burton brewing heritage and its mission of “bringing mates together”. In the last decade or…
BrandOpus has refreshed the much-loved lager brand with a football-style crest celebrating its Burton brewing heritage and its mission of “bringing mates together”.

In the last decade or so, it feels like every British brand has tried to link itself with British football. But some have been in the game, so to speak, longer than others. And if you’re looking for authentic ties, you’ll struggle to find a better example than Carling.

For decades now, it’s been in the hands of fans on matchday, and despite the inexorable rise of hipster craft beers, this honest, reliable, easy-drinking, thirst-quenching amber nectar of a drink (can you tell it’s my favourite tipple?) still gets great love from the football crowd today.

That love has long been two-way. Carling’s name has been on cup competitions, club hoardings and more than a few pub chalkboards for as long as I can remember. And in 2026, they’re leaning into that more than ever, with a refreshed identity built around a football-style badge.

Now rolling out now across supermarkets, convenience stores, pubs and bars, the new identity, crafted by BrandOpus, aims to reimagine Carling’s role in modern culture through the language of community, quality and heritage.

At the heart of the refresh is the new badge, which evokes a sense of the crests stitched onto football shirts. The aim was to make drinking Carling feel more like being part of a team. As Paul Taylor, CCO and co-founder at BrandOpus, explains: “The creative strategy was built around Carling’s core brand purpose of bringing mates together, with all design elements crafted to convey moments of connection.

“Long used in football and communities as a symbol of shared identity, pride and connection, the badge is deployed as a visual metaphor for belonging. It reconnects Carling with its roots, while tying it back to the world of football. It makes the brand feel like a club that people are a part of.”
One good way to convey community and belonging visually is through symbols of heritage and history, and the new design is packed with those.

Inside the badge are illustrations of the historic Carling Brewery and the Burton Bridge, framed by sprigs of barley, with “The Carling Brewery” and “Burton-upon-Trent” threaded around the edge, and Carling’s Black Label banner running across the middle.
For good measure, BrandOpus also added the signature of founder and original brewer Thomas Carling to the can and the glass.

The new pint glass builds on the existing design, which BrandOpus previously helped craft as part of their long-running partnership. This version dials up the heritage messaging with the new badge, along with embossed Burton-upon-Trent lettering near the base.

BrandOpus has also developed a wider, flexible brand world that builds on Carling’s long relationship with football, from grassroots clubs to the Emirates FA Cup and the Women’s FA Cup. This includes a set of illustrated murals and out-of-home assets for stadiums and club sites, designed to adapt to each club’s colours and personality.

All this seems like a smart move for a brand that’s been around for a long time and risks being taken for granted. After all, people’s attitudes to both beer and football have changed dramatically over the past decade, and it feels like the sands are constantly shifting: incoming Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s focus on relaxing the drinking laws at football grounds stands testament to that.
Carling needed to respond to both shifts, reasserting its place in a crowded market while strengthening its ties with the game and the communities around it.

As Ryan McLaughlin, brand director for Carling at Molson Coors, puts it: “This is much more than a packaging refresh. As consumer expectations continue to evolve, it’s important that iconic brands evolve too.

“This is the latest step in Carling’s evolution, building on the strengths that have made it the leading core lager brand in Great Britain, while creating a bolder, more contemporary identity for the future.”
Show, don’t tell: Father explains what it does, with a film that lets the coastline do the talking
The London creative studio took hydrophones and contact mics to Kent’s coast to make a short film titled Can You Hear This?. As long as I’ve been using TikTok – which at this point seems…
The London creative studio took hydrophones and contact mics to Kent’s coast to make a short film titled Can You Hear This?.

As long as I’ve been using TikTok – which at this point seems like a lifetime – my guilty pleasure has been that meme that goes “Tell me you’re a something, without telling me you’re a something”. Most of these videos are pretty vapid, but there’s a fundamental point to the meme that I very much vibe with: the principle of “show, don’t tell”.

In other words, whether you’re creating a poster, a trailer, a website or any other type of design, don’t waste your audience’s time with a lot of dull explanation. Try to convey your message visually instead, in a way that lands as simply and quickly as possible.

Sometimes, though, the subject matter isn’t so easy to convey in a visual. Take for instance, this conundrum: how do you tell me you’re a creative studio specialising in sound without telling me you’re a creative studio specialising in sound?
For London-based Father, the answer was to head to Dungeness, one of the strangest and most atmospheric corners of the English coast, fire up some mics, and start listening.
The result is a short film entitled Can You Hear This?.

Armed with hydrophones and contact microphones, the team spent time recording sounds from the shingle landscape. They then set up a mobile studio on location and spent several days turning what they’d heard into music.

In a media landscape dominated by noise, the film is a refreshingly quiet, slow watch, as the camera moves between wind-blown marshland and the glowing knobs of analogue synths. Best of all, it’s free from the kind of overbearing narration you might expect. “We think of it as an unspoken manifesto,” says Father co-founder Joe Farley. “Some of what matters most about how we work is hard to put into words, so we wanted people to feel it instead.”

So how did they get here? Composers Joe and Freddie Webb started out as runners in Soho, playing in a band together on the side, until one day a director asked them to write music for the British Fashion Council. More than a decade on, their collaboration has grown into a creative studio that mixes musical craft with design thinking and strategy.

Alongside the film, the launch includes an evolved visual identity by branding agency Further and a collection of designed objects. In December, it continues with a limited vinyl release designed in collaboration with Tom Hingston, founder of Hingston Studio , and a listening session at Space Talk, a hi-fi listening bar on St John Street, on London’s Farringdon/Clerkenwell border.

“With Chapter 01, we wanted to show that even as we’ve grown, craft and artistry remain at the heart of Father,” says the studio’s managing director, Aifric Lennon. “We move naturally between an exhibition at the V&A and a sonic identity for O2, and what we explore in one feeds what we bring to the other.”

At the heart of both the studio and the film is a belief that sound shouldn’t be something tacked on at the end of a project, but a design material in its own right. In Can You Hear This?, that’s interpreted literally: the music grows directly out of the sounds of the place.

“For us, sound is something you design with from the very beginning,” stresses Freddie. “We treat it with the same intention and creative rigour as every other element of design: light, colour, material, texture, movement and space. Rhythm, tone and silence can all shape how something feels and functions.”

You can hear that approach across the studio’s portfolio. For the V&A exhibition Schiaparelli: Fashion Becomes Art , Father worked with architecture and design studio Nebbia on a series of scores built from recordings of materials and processes. Running through them is a repeated fragment of Debussy: something visitors sense they’ve heard before, without quite being able to place it.

For O2 , meanwhile, a recording session centred on the sound of human breath became the starting point for a sonic identity and brand track. And for cycling clothing and accessory brand Rapha , the studio created a set of interconnected original tracks that form a distinctive musical language…

Thelma Golden Stepping Down as Studio Museum Director After 21 Years
The pathbreaking museum leader has guided the museum through its momentous rebuild and mentored generations of Black artists and curators.

One year after the Studio Museum in Harlem's long-awaited reopening , Thelma Golden, 61, intends to step down after 21 years as the institution's director and chief curator. Golden will depart both roles once the museum appoints a replacement.

“I know this is the right moment to begin this transition — and as I look ahead to new projects and opportunities, I also look back with gratitude toward the many people whose achievements have been my bedrock,” Golden said in a press statement regarding her decision.

Since assuming both titles in 2005, Golden has stimulated international and institutional recognition of Black, African, and diasporic African artists who are systematically overlooked in the Western canons of art history and modern and contemporary art. Prior to joining the Studio Museum, then led by Lowery Stokes Sims, Golden held curatorial roles at the Whitney Museum of American Art.

A new site design and wordmark for Hyperallergic’s next era.

From the start in 2009, Hyperallergic has been kicking at the doors of the art world status quo, challenging assumptions about what is worthy of investigation and investment, and the supposed neutrality of those decisions. Today, 17 years later, we are no longer a young upstart blogazine but a daily source of trusted news, reviews, and opinions for millions in the art community.

We’ve transformed our strategy for sustainable revenue and evolved our editorial approach several times over the years to meet the unique challenges of each internet era. While so many of our peers have disappeared, we’ve survived as an independent media company throughout it all. It’s never been easy, but it’s always been worth it.

As we enter yet another new era, with social media becoming ever more toxic and AI seemingly overtaking every aspect of our lives, we want to refocus ourselves on being the best place for our community to gather. For all of us to learn, to grow, to laugh, and to feel connected to each other.
Today, we are excited to introduce the next transformation of this site, with a whole new look, a dynamic homepage, and the third version of our wordmark.

It’s clear that the insistent and demanding bright cyan of the site is no longer needed, and it is time for Hyperallergic to look more like the authoritative publication it has now become. (And for those who always loved the blue, you’ll see it re-emerge in spots over time.)

The Brooklyn-based design cooperative, Partner & Partners , has created a warm and inviting new look and organizational framework that fits our evolving output and will help us expand into the future.

Our new wordmark is drawn from Hyperallergic TwoOneFive, a new custom typeface made for us by Commercial Type . It is a grotesque that harkens back to the days of the Bauhaus and is full of unique quirks that push it into the future. Letting go of the uppercase blue condensed wordmark, the new logotype leans towards classic while remaining full of energy. The high bar of the capital H leads us into the lowercase title; this itself is a marker that we no longer need the screech of all caps.

Hyperallergic is by and for art-focused readers and writers, so the site has to encourage both. Spectator, a new serif typeface also from Commercial Type, brings a richness and warmth to the screen. Compared with more traditional typefaces, Spectator is clean with soft corners and is bolder all around, encouraging the eye to move from line to line.
We’re foregrounding our authors' names to highlight our team and many guest contributors, and the effort and care that goes into all the work you see on the site.

With a vast archive of tens of thousands of posts from thousands of writers and spanning nearly two decades, we’ve built a whole new search experience and a reorganized tagging system to allow readers to discover connections between writers, themes, and subjects that might otherwise get lost.
This new site design allows for more diversity in article layouts and lets us give prominence on our homepage to stories we think deserve more of your attention.

But ultimately, one of the design’s strongest elements is its ability to get out of the way. While vastly improving the user experience, it rarely draws attention to itself, instead allowing the focus to be on the content of the site, rather than the frame.

This redesign is just one part of a bigger shift. You may have noticed we now ask you to sign in to a free account to read most articles. That’s because we want to build a closer relationship with our readers and a more sustainable platform to publish the news, reviews, and commentary that keep you engaged, informed, inspired, and entertained. All while speaking truth and challenging the status quo in the art world.

Open-source tools like Ghost allow us to remain insulated from the whims of platforms funded by venture capital, with sky-high investments and unrealistic valuations that inevitably force them to pivot or shut down. Tools like these have allowed us to keep publishing without fear for the past 17 years and invest in what matters most: connecting our writers to our readers.
When a Ceramics Studio Becomes a Stage
In Matthew Lutz-Kinoy’s "The Mud Room," the gallery acts as a site of production.

At the center of Matthew Lutz-Kinoy’s The Mud Room, a raised platform containing a large kiln, two ceramicists’ alcoves, and buckets of clay acts as a stage. The first play explored the intersections of farming, the kiln, and the emergence of the artspeak-adjacent locavore chef.

While Amant’s on-site restaurant served its own fare of purple radicchio and Block Island anchovies to the audience, seated in a perimeter around the action, the protagonist, Marin — a failed curator turned restaurateur in rural France — droned on about her hopes for a publisher to appreciate her culinary foray as a radical “linguistic concept” and “rhizomatic” project.

Meanwhile, four paintings surrounding the stage ridicule the posturing of the art-world types in the first performance. Directly opposite the entrance, monstrous figures swallow one another’s entrails and phallic appendages while exchanging the fruits of their labor: ceramics. To the right, Lutz-Kinoy’s “The Rose Garden” (2026) combines an homage to Keith Haring’s “Crack Is Wack” (1986) with silhouettes reminiscent of Aaron Douglas’s New Deal-era public commissions. Opposite it, another painting pays tribute to Douglas, as well as to Philip Guston and Reuben Kadish’s restored “The Struggle Against War and Fascism” (1934–35).

South African Curator and Artist Tamlin Blake Murdered at 51
Tap the button below for the full story.
Visionary curator and mixed-media artist Tamlin Blake was found murdered in her Riebeek West home in South Africa on Sunday, November 22, at age 51.

West Coast District police confirmed that several of Blake's items were allegedly stolen and traced to a nearby farm. The 32-year-old suspect, who police have since arrested, had been released from prison less than a week before the incident, according to local outlets .

As the chief curator at Spier Arts Trust, a Cape Town-based nonprofit dedicated to connecting South African artists with larger audiences and collectors, Blake conceived programs to help artists advance their careers. An artist herself, she explored themes of belonging, identity, and status in multiple exhibitions at Everard Read gallery , and fostered collaborations with the Spier Artisan Studio and the Keiskamma Art Project.

“Tamlin was pivotal in helping me find my artistic identity, guiding me with honesty, kindness and insight,” Madeleine van Manen, who was Blake’s mentee under the Spier Arts Trust’s Creative Block program in 2016, told Hyperallergic . “With every new experiment I knew I could rely on her input to make the best of it.”
How Alison Luchs, the “Museum Rizzler,” Became Gen Z’s Goated Art Historian
The National Gallery of Art's 78-year-old Early European sculpture curator and designated baddie gives us the deets on how she became a social media superstar overnight.

Lock in, chat, because we're about to drop some major lore on a new internet personality who puts every influencer to shame. During a recent kiki with Hyperallergic , designated baddie Alison Luchs, a curator of Early European sculpture and Deputy Head of Sculpture and Decorative Arts at the National Gallery of Art (NGA) in Washington, DC, gave us the deets on how she became a social media superstar overnight by using Gen Z lingo in an educational video series about collection objects.

This has been a goated year for Luchs, who has worked with the NGA for over four decades. Now known as the “Museum Rizzler,” the 78-year-old curator has garnered millions of views on her videos translating art and anthropological history into accessible stories for younger generations. Connecting centuries-old artifacts and mythologies to contemporary pop culture with terms like “chopped,” “sigma,” “aura points,” “gagged,” “popping off,” “chud,” and so on, Luchs has drawn a reverent audience that gassed her up so much she was honored with two Webby Awards .

Luchs and NGA's head of marketing and communications, Sydni Myers, broke down the making of the Museum Rizzler, the virtual and in-person impacts of the series' instant virality, and the behind-the-scenes process that goes into each video. This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
Kate Jenkins Whips Up Delicious ‘Knitalian’ Dishes in an Immersive Exhibition
Have you ever considered the mouthwatering possibilities of yarn?

From plates of ravioli and spaghetti to bottles of chianti and sardines springing from their tins, Kate Jenkins ‘ immersive art-meets-restaurant experience is something to really sink your teeth into. Known for her realistic knitted foodstuffs , the Brighton-based artist and knitwear designer presents Kate’s Knitalian at Air Contemporary , inviting us to consider the (rather unexpected) mouthwatering possibilities of yarn.

For the opening reception, visitors were required to reserve a spot much as one would do to book a table in a traditional restaurant, including two timed sittings. Everything from wheels of salami and tortellini to tiramisù and bottles of “Pinot Stitchio” fill the delicatessen experience in a celebration of Italian cuisine.

Kate’s Knitalian continues through December 22 in London. And if you find yourself in Brighton, you can visit the artist’s studio, which is open daily in Arundel Place. See more on Jenkins’ Instagram . You might also enjoy Lucy Sparrow’s The Beginning of Convenience, an entirely felted supermarket at The Momentary in Bentonville, Arkansas.
Design Miami 2026 Preview: “Unveiling” Works From 75 International Galleries at This Year’s Miami Art Week

Design Miami 2026 Preview: “Unveiling” Works From 75 International Galleries at This Year’s Miami Art Week
Brodin, “Constellation of Memory,” 2026. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Kelley and Gavin Brodin.)

Design Miami , one of the most exciting events of Miami Art Week, is back for the 22nd edition of its flagship fair. The event, devoted to contemporary collectible design, returns to the Miami Beach Convention Center with a lineup of 75 international galleries, museum-quality presentations, and a curatorial theme that celebrates the creatives behind the works on display.

The theme, Unveiling , calls for the viewers to truly observe each object, deciphering what inspired the artist to create them, and the surrounding stories behind their choices. These may be hiding in plain sight or several times removed from the final result, reflecting something deeply personal or rooted in the artist’s culture. Unveiling is then divided among four curatorial threads, each with different approaches and best represented by certain artists, techniques, and galleries.
Design Miami is back with with a lineup of 75 international galleries and a curatorial theme that celebrates the creatives behind the works on display.
Pippin Drysdale, “Sacred Lands,” 2026. Adrian Sassoon at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Adrian Sassoon, London; photography by Robert Frith, Acorn Photo.)

First up is Process as Aesthetic: Unveiling the Hand of the Maker . This theme highlights the creative process, particularly the techniques, labor, and experimentation that come to determine an object’s aesthetic, regarding these steps as a vehicle for expression. This can be seen in the ceramic works of Bouke de Vries and Pippin Drysdale; Caroline Desile’s architecture-influenced Totem 1 ; Richard Haining’s STACKED creations, made up of thousands of pieces of salvaged New York City wood; and Man Ray’s Optic-Topic mask , the centerpiece of this division.
Le Corbusier, “La licorne passe sur la mer,” 1959. Boccara Gallery at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Boccara Gallery.)

Meanwhile, Subverting Archetypes: The Familiar, Reimagined , takes a more surrealist route, blurring the line between the familiar and the uncanny, asking viewers to reassess to what they think they know. Such is the case of a selection of 20th-century tapestries by Le Corbusier, Sonia Delaunay, and Alexander Calder. This section also features the work of Brazilian designer Lucas Recchia, who blends metal with fused glass, and a wall piece by Jaydan Moore, who turns found, silver-plated tableware into sculptural forms.
Dee Clements, “Gams,” 2026. Mindy Solomon Gallery at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: Clare Britt, courtesy of the artist and Mindy Solomon Gallery)
Prateek Jain & Gautam Seth, “Enchanted Forest,” 2025. Klove Studio at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of klove.)
Glover, “A Natural History of Dreams,” 2022. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Duane Reed Gallery.)

Material poetry: Unveiling material potential explores the expectations materials carry, alongside their emotional, sensory, and imaginative possibilities. This is best represented by the work of Dutch designer Frederik Molenschot and Franco-Swedish designer Ingrid Donat, with the former approaching bronze as heavy and imposing, and the latter as luminous and weightless. Fernando Mastrangelo also touches on this with a monolithic sculpture cast from glass and sand that conceals an expandable cabinet within its architectural form.
KAMEH by Nikita Erokhin, “Beyond Reflection,” 2026. KAMEH at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Nikita Berezhnoy.)
Cure, “Color in Suspension,” 2026. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Laura Hernandez.)
Barford, Light Sculpture “Feast,” 2026. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of David Gill Gallery)

Finally, Mirrors of Society and Place: Unveiling Identity, Culture, and Locality assesses how design can convey identity, values, culture, and collective memory. After all, objects can become reflections of the societies and environments from which they emerge. British street artist Helen Bur completes her largest mural to date in Bordeaux's Grand Parc neighbourhood, celebrating motherhood, female solidarity and community connection through EXIT's…

British street artist Helen Bur has completed her largest mural to date in Bordeaux, France, transforming the towering façade of the Nerval residential building in the Grand Parc neighbourhood into a monumental portrait of motherhood, female solidarity and human connection. Entitled Matrescense , the artwork depicts two local women in the final trimester of pregnancy, brought together through a project that celebrates the importance of companionship and mutual support within the community.
Helen Bur, WIP, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The title, Matrescence , refers to the profound transition into motherhood, a developmental process encompassing the physical, psychological, emotional and social changes experienced as a woman becomes a mother. Much like adolescence, it is a period of transformation in which identity, relationships and perceptions of self evolve.

Through her portrayal of two expectant mothers, Helen Bur gives this often overlooked experience a monumental public presence, recognising not only the vulnerability and anticipation of pregnancy but also the importance of connection, understanding and mutual support during one of life’s most significant transitions.
Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Created for KIFKIF, an ambitious urban art initiative led by Bordeaux-based association EXIT, the mural marks the beginning of a wider programme connecting internationally recognised artists with local residents through public art, creative workshops and community participation.

At the heart of Matrescense are two pregnant women arranged head-to-foot, their bodies forming an intimate, almost circular composition reminiscent of the yin-yang symbol. One reclines towards the ground while the other turns upwards, their opposing positions creating a sense of balance and interdependence. Although each woman occupies her own space within the painting, their gestures and proximity suggest an unspoken relationship built upon understanding, companionship and mutual care.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Both women live in Bordeaux’s Grand Parc neighbourhood and were invited to become models for the artwork. Remarkably, they had not known one another before the project, making their connection something that developed through the creative process itself. What appears to be a longstanding bond between two women was, in fact, formed through the experience of participating in the mural.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The subject emerged from Helen Bur’s exploration of the neighbourhood’s social realities, particularly the experiences of women raising children without a partner. Rather than portraying motherhood through an idealised image of the family, she places two expectant mothers together, acknowledging the friendships, relationships and wider networks of support that can become essential throughout pregnancy and parenthood.
Matrescense: Intimacy on a Monumental Scale

Rising across the façade of the Nerval building, the 32-metre mural transforms an ordinary residential elevation into an expansive, deeply personal painting. Completed following more than two weeks on site, despite challenging weather conditions, the work represents a significant milestone in Bur’s artistic practice.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The composition is particularly striking for the contrast between its monumental scale and the intimacy of its subject. The two women appear suspended within a richly layered interior of deep terracotta, warm ochre and patterned textiles, surrounded by abundant green foliage. The arrangement creates the impression of a private domestic space opened to the city, allowing an everyday moment of connection to occupy the architecture of an entire building.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

OUTSIDE IN: New Exhibition at GraffitiStreet Gallery, Chichester
What happens when art made for walls, rooftops and railway lines comes indoors? OUTSIDE IN brings internationally recognised street artists to GraffitiStreet Gallery, Chichester, exploring…

What happens when art made for walls, rooftops and railway lines comes indoors? This November 20th, GraffitiStreet Gallery presents OUTSIDE IN, a group exhibition bringing together internationally recognised artists whose practices are rooted in graffiti and street art. Exploring the journey from public space to the studio, the exhibition considers how an artist’s distinctive visual language moves between different settings, scales and materials, and how these transitions change the way we experience their work.

A graffiti tag, a mural spanning a building, a canvas contained within a frame and a sculpture within the gallery each create a different encounter with the viewer. Site can amplify or redirect meaning, scale can alter our response, and material can reveal another dimension of an artist’s practice. Yet across these shifts, the symbols, ideas and signature styles that define each artist remain unmistakable. How much of urban art is bound to its setting, and how much travels with the artist?
As the street enters the gallery, OUTSIDE IN invites visitors to discover what changes, what intensifies and what endures.

German artist Case Maclaim , a pioneer of photorealist graffiti, moves between monumental murals and intimate studio paintings, bringing the technical precision and extraordinary attention to detail that have defined his practice into a more concentrated setting.

Spanish duo PichiAvo unite classical sculpture and graffiti, bringing ancient mythology into dialogue with contemporary urban culture. Their distinctive compositions challenge the boundaries between artistic traditions, allowing the language of the street to coexist with the enduring influence of classical art.

South African artist Faith47 , internationally recognised for her poetic large-scale murals, extends her practice into sculpture, exploring how familiar themes and imagery acquire a different physical presence through material and form.

British artist My Dog Sighs transforms overlooked objects and unconventional surfaces into emotionally resonant artworks, while Sweet Toof brings the irreverence of his unmistakable teeth motif into paintings that connect graffiti, portraiture and art history.

Belgian artist Joachim Lambrechts balances spontaneous mark-making with carefully considered compositions, while South African artist Sonny Sundancer explores the expressive possibilities of abstraction beyond his large-scale street practice. Nean Kingdom , whose distinctive imagery has become an instantly recognisable part of his artistic identity, similarly demonstrates how a visual language developed through street art can retain its character in the studio.

Although their approaches differ considerably, each artist offers a perspective on the relationship between artistic identity and environment. Moving between the street and the studio becomes more than a change of location; it creates opportunities to experiment with materials, reconsider scale and develop ideas beyond the conditions in which their practices first emerged.
An Exhibition Across Materials and Disciplines

Alongside the featured artists, OUTSIDE [IN] includes selected artworks and collectables by Banksy, STIK and TOX, bringing further dimensions to the exhibition’s exploration of graffiti and street art.

From the repetition of a graffiti tag to the intimacy of a painting, the exhibition reveals how urban art continues to evolve across disciplines while retaining its connection to the visual culture of the street.

Together, these diverse practices create an opportunity to experience familiar artistic languages in an entirely different context, encouraging visitors to look beyond the surface and consider the ideas, techniques and identities that give each artist’s work its distinctive character.
